As someone who was an anthropology major but with experience in biomedical sexual and reproductive health, I found his insight particularly interesting and relevant to discussions surrounding structural violence and how that then plays out in public health.Here are my ideas for interventions:1) Peer EducationWhen I interned with UNFPA in Costa Rica, one program they had in place was the training of peer educators in rural, northern areas where many Nicaraguan immigrants reside. This is a population that faces discrimination, and so they are that much more at risk for HIV infection. The program focused on teenagers, since as we all know, young women are contracting HIV at a very rapid rate. I saw how these teens, armed with knowledge but also an innate understanding of how their communities functioned, went around spreading information and providing opportunities to discuss these important matters. These peer educators received a boost of self esteem by being the ones to help their friends. The families were also very proud, as I personally saw when I got to know one young woman who was an educator in her town. This also relates back to empowering women, and especially younger ones.2) Another related line of intervention is to provide spaces to explore structural inequalities in places where this is not often done. I grew up in a place where we did talk about sexism and such, but I know that this is not the norm for everyone. In one workshop we completed in Costa Rica, we looked at body image with young women and discussed messages we received from the media, our families, etc. and then translated those messages to how we felt and behaved. This was not a line of thinking that this particular group was accustomed to, but they were very engaged and interested in debating it amongst themselves. The market for housing in San Francisco is NOT efficient in pareto standards. In this situation, it is not impossible to make one person better off without hurting another person. The enforcement of rent control places a price ceiling on the market to make housing more affordable to people who cannot typically afford more expensive housing. This means that the marginal benefit to consumers is not equal to the marginal cost for producers (the benefit of the last unit produced is not equal to the cost of that unit), therefore, creating an inefficient market. Additionally, the producers of more expensive housing will not be able to sell their housing at appropriate prices, resulting in a deadweight loss. This is lost surplus for the suppliers as the buyers are benefitted. There is not an easy way to keep prices low in an efficient market, because there will always be plenty of people willing to pay the ceiling price and the producers that produce at these prices will have little incentive to lower their quality of production.

Here's a simple example: Suppose A is rolling a die and getting 6, and B is it raining in Stanford tomorrow. If I tell you that A occurred, that does not give you any additional information to predict whether it will rain in Stanford tomorrow! Thus, A & B are independent.But if I tell you that A has occurred, you can say with certainty that ~A has NOT occurred. Romain, you are working through the course very quickly! Yes, beta coefficients can be a huge source of confusion when authors/readers do not pay close enough attention to the units. Beta coefficients are entirely unit-dependent, so you have to think very carefully about the units. However, they do have some advantages over correlation coefficients. We often want to know how much does Y increase or decrease on average for a 1-unit increase in X. The correlation coefficient does not tell us this. A good alternative, for continuous variables, is to standardize them by turning them into Z-scores (Standard Deviation units). If you put standardized variables into the linear regression model, then the beta coefficients will be in SD-Y/SD-X units. So for example, a beta coefficient of 0.25 tells that a 1-SD increase in X correlates to a 0.25-SD increase in Y. It's easier to compare across different predictors if they are all in SD units.

Once you have this conditional probability law, then it's trivial to construct the Bayes classifier. But in real life you only get a sample of data from a population! You do not know which are the distributions that generated it. Sometimes, that's exactly one of the things you would like to find out! In the case of LDA, for example, you *assume* that the $f_k(x)$ are normal and share a common standard deviation, but you do not know for sure. Also, you have no idea which are the means $mu_k$ and standard deviation $sigma$ of these (assumed) normal distributions, and you do not know which are the $pi_k$. Of course you can *estimate* them from data, but you do not know for sure.By the way, one of the examples where LDA got so close to the Bayes Classifier was an example with two classes,where $f_1(x)$ and $f_2(x)$ were *chosen* to be normal with the same standard deviation. That's also a reason why LDA did so well :)

There will be some bias in the estimate of the MSE if you are both tuning the model *and* estimating the MSE at the same time.Double CV is often used when you need to tune *and* estimate the model. Essentially you have an outer CV loop, say a $k$-fold with $k = 5$, and then within each fold you do an entire CV (another $k$-fold for example or a bootstrap CV). The inner fold is to choose the values of the parameters you want to tune (number of components etc) and then you fit the tuned model and use it to predict for the fold left out in the outer loop. Repeat for all folds in the outer loop.That said, it is my understanding that the bias in tuning *and* estimating the error at the same time is not that large in many cases. Whether that bias is larger or smaller than the bias introduced by fitting CV models to even smaller subsets of the training data is something I cannot answer.

Assume that the NBA's only purpose is to maximize revenue and profits, and that revenue and profits are maximized when games are played by the best available basketball players. In the absence of any rule, available players will make decisions about the value of playing basketball and the value of going to college, which is the opportunity cost of choosing professional basketball. With a rule that potential players must sit out one year after high school, the value to a player of playing in the NBA for that year is zero, and the value of attending college for one year is no longer the opportunity cost of playing in the NBA in that year, which is not an alternative. If the value of attending college for one year is greater than the value of some alternative activity, a player will attend college. However, the players for whom the value of a basketball career is much more valuable than a career whose vlaue is enhanced by attending college will leave college after one year. Hence, the only effect of the rule is likely to be that the NBA reduces the availability of the best players by one year. With a rule that potential players must sit out until they have graduated from college, available players must make a decision between the value of going to college and then playing in the NBA and the value of pursuing some alternative career, the new opportunity cost of playing in the NBA. Under that rule, players unable to graduate from college do not have the possibility of playing in the NBA, and assuming the absence of these players reduces the NBA revenue, the rule simply harms the NBA's interests, and the interests of potential players. For players able to graduate from college, and for whom a career being paid to play basketball is much more valuable than a career whose value is enhanced by attending college, the rule simply reduces the value of their basketball career by four or perhaps more years. For the NBA, the absence of those players while they are attending college probably reduces NBA revenue and does so to a much larger extent than the one year rule, and would appear to be in the NBA's interests only if 4 plus years of college basketball experience enhances a player's ability during a shortened NBA career, or allows the NBA better to select players by evaluating them based on their college careers.

The enforcement of rent control in the San Francisco housing market is not Pareto efficient because it is still possible to allocate resources while not making another worse off. Consumers have a larger marginal benefit as they can afford more luxurious apartments thanks to the price control while producers do not have such a great benefit in producing great apartments. This leads to a shortage in housing as there is not a great incentive for producers to increase the supply of housing. The price ceiling can lead to a large deadweight loss in the housing market and show the inefficiency of the market. The only way to keep the price of housing low and create an efficient market is to lower the fixed costs for the producers such as costs for permits to build or property taxes. This would give producers an incentive to increase the housing supply and create a more efficient market.However,this is unlikely to happen so in reality there is no perfect way to bring the market into pareto efficiency except by removing government intervention and letting the market bring itself to pareto efficiency.

We do not use ability grouping for math in my school. Two years ago, in 3rd grade (which is the grade I teach) our administrator asked the 3rd grade team to split our students by ability for reading. We did this for several reasons, but primarily because we had to document for RTI (Response to Intervention) for those students reading below grade level. We used several tools to determine where to place children and the children were never told that they were being \grouped\", just that we were changing teachers for reading groups. [And, yes, some of them could figure out what we were doing.] The groups were fluid, however, so that if a child made significant progress in reading ability, he or she was \"moved\" to another teacher (essentially another/higher group). What we discovered was that those children who were so very low that they could not read was that once they were placed in a very small class, they began to participate more AND their reading difficulties became more obvious. Why? Because suddenly those children could not disappear into the larger group. They felt more at ease responding because they were in the same boat as everyone else at the reading table. Most of those children made huge strides in their reading levels.As a teacher I noticed that even though we used several tools, some children were incorrectly placed. The students in my class were reading way beyond the 3rd grade level and were considered the advanced group; however, some of those students simply did not have the maturity to be in such a class and found themselves way over their heads.I know this is not about math and I recognize the problems with grouping or labeling; however, I see the benefits for those 3rd graders who are so woefully behind in their reading skills. They need that small group setting--those intervention strategies to bring them up to speed."

You may have noticed that some functions in R do different things depending on the class of argument you pass. For example, if x is a numeric vector plot(x) does something different from what it does if x is a lm fit. This works because plot is what's called a \generic\" function with multiple \"methods\" (think of these as different behaviors it can have) for different data types. There are two ways that you can write generic functions in R. One is by using \"S3 methods\" and the other is by using \"S4 methods.\" Unless you plan to write your own R package, the differences are not really important. What matters to an end user is that if you see \"S3 method\" in the documentation of a function, then there is a generic function that calls that function for particular types of data. For example, plot.lm is the S3 method that the generic function plot calls in order to show the diagnostic plots for an lm object.Hope that helps."

The thing about GDP is that it measures a very specific thing. Specifically, it measures the total amount of production in a country. Realize that, because the real world is not perfectly competitive, and because big markets tend towards oligopoly, there is often a surplus of products produced, creating deadweight loss while technically increasing the statistic of GDP. If we define GDP as Y = C + I + G + (X-M), then increased consumption could increase the statistic. This is the intended aim of stimulus spending and low interest rates, which hope to encourage more people to consume. However, the amount that the government spends is also counted into the GDP. Think of WWII. While the average person was not so well off, the statistic of GDP went sky high simply because of the high government spending on the war. GDP does not measure the theoretical maximum-efficiency scenario; by definition, the government will be less Pareto-efficient than the market in its purchases.Overall, the measure of quality of life can be determined with the Human Development Index (HDI). Some people propose the Gini coefficient (a measure of inequality), but realistically, a country can have high inequality and still be well-off. Even the poorest citizens of the US survive on more money than the rest of the world. Of course, the cost of living also factors into this. The HDI takes all of this into consideration, and as a result, the highest-scoring nations are the wealthy Scandanavian, Western European, and Australian countries.

Q: At the same submaximal workload on an exercise bike before and after endurance training, you will use:A: The same amount of oxygen.The concept of a submax workload and oxygen consumption is tricky, and often students in our class at Stanford have trouble with it before it clicks. So know your confusion is in good company. Lets see if I can be helpful. The main point is this: **it requires the same amount of oxygen for your body to do a certain amount of work.** If that work is below the maximal capacity, we call it a submax workload. For example, I did a few months of cycling training to increase my aerobic fitness a year or so back as a part of a previous teaching project. We tested my VO2max by doing a progressive (increasing workload every few minutes) test on a stationary bike where I wore a mask that measured the oxygen I was using at Week 0, Week 5, and Week 10 of my training regimen. My VO2max increased across my 10 week training program because my body had optimized components of the fick equation, meaning that I could finish the test at a later stage where I cycled at higher watts of resistance. Lets say at Week 0 my maximum resistance at the end of the test was 250 watts, but at Week 10 it was 350 watts. Because of my training, I was becoming a better cyclist! Here is the point. Regardless of my training and assuming my cycling technique did not change, at 150 watts (a light, submaximal workload), my body needed to consume the same amount of oxygen at Week 0 Week 5 and Week 10 to do 150 watts of work. The difference is, at the end of the training, my body could consume more oxygen, and 150 watts of a submaximal workload was easier because it was a lower percentage of my overall VO2max. -Staff

Because additional trees are fitted to the *residuals* of the current fit. When the first tree is grown it is trying to fit the response as the response values are copied to the residuals vector. Then, a simple tree is fitted and a shrunken version of the fitted values is taken as the contribution of that tree to the fit. The residuals are reduced by the same amount, ready for the next tree.When the second tree is grown, because each tree is fitted to the *residuals* (**not** the observed values of the response), the fit is improved some more and with it the bias is reduced a little bit; the two trees more closely follow the data than the first tree alone.As you keep adding trees, those trees explain aspects of the data not well fitted by the set of previously fitted trees. If you were to keep on fitting, eventually you'd explain all the variance in the data: the residuals would be reduced to zero, and hence there'd be *no* bias [but high variance at that point]. Achieving this takes a long time with boosted trees because of the shrinkage applied to the fitted values of each tree; hence boosted trees learn slowly.Contrast this with randomForests; there we have the same ensemble of trees, but each tree is fitted to the same response vector of data/observations. The stochasticity introduced via bagging and the random selection of `mtry` parameters for each split-selection reduces models that can be averaged over, to reduce variance.I cannot quite think of a good way to explain what is happening to the bias in a randomForest; you are fitting a (potentially) low bias, high variance tree to a bootstrap sample of the data because you grow each tree large, but as you only consider random subsets of the available variables to form each split in those trees, they could still be biased. How the two sources of bias contribute to the actual bias of the tree and hence to the ensemble of trees I am not sure about. Perhaps someone will comment?

Sure. No problem. As to the CLT and the irreducible errors, I guess I was making a subtle distinction in a not very clear way. Expecting the irreducible errors to be typically be nearly normal by an appeal to the CLT as stated in the wikipedia article is sort of a philosophical choice...but it should be checked to see if they really are in any given situation. And if they are not, gathering more data probably will not make them that way. The data generating mechanism either has noise that is a sum of independent random jolts or it does not. On the other hand, gathering more data will tend to make the sampling distribution of the parameters more normal by the CLT because they are estimated as sums of the observed responses weighted by combinations of the observed explanatory variables. So as long as the irreducible errors are not from some pathological distribution that the CLT does not apply to, we can expect the betas to be distributed normally if we gather enough data.

If we had a two-sided null, then all you check is, is the null hypothesis value within the confidence interval. As she said in lecture, if it does, then you cannot reject the null. If it does not then you can. If the null hypothesis is one-sided, things are a little different. Being in the confidence interval still means you cannot reject, but now, if you are outside of the interval, it makes a difference which side you are on. That's because being more than 1.96 standard errors in one direction is not an unexpected result (the data is not too unusual), while being more than 1.96 standard errors in the other direction is unexpected or unusual. I am using 1.96 because it's a 95% confidence interval.If the null is, $$p_0 > 0.20$$Then being bigger than the confidence interval does not seem unusual. It's more than 1.96 SE's above 0.20 but the null is not saying 0.20 is the correct value, just that the correct value is no smaller than 0.2, the real value could be bigger and then your sample would not be unusual. In that direction, we are saying our sample value is no greater than 1.96 SE's from the true value.Now, suppose your sample gives a value that is more than 1.96 SE's below 0.20 . That's unusual, as since the true value is assumed to be no smaller than 0.20, we are at least 1.96 SE's from the true value.

I think the resolution is that consumers have a wide variety of options of products on which to spend their money.For example, say I am a consumer who has 10 dollars to spend.There is a product X that costs 4 dollars / unit has a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.If, as a consumer with a 10 dollar budget, product X is the only product available for me to purchase in the market, I will maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing two of product X for a total utility of 8 dollars.However, let's introduce a product Y that costs 4 dollars / unit and has a marginal benefit of 4 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 2 dollars for 2 units purchased.Now, as a consumer, I can maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing 1 unit of product X and 1 unit of product Y for a total utility of 9 dollars.If either product X or product Y exists in isolation, my maximum utility is achieved by purchasing two units of the product. However, if both of these products exist together in the market -- a good model of the real world -- then I will purchase one of each.In general, a purchase can be thought of as a transaction of value, and consumers will optimize utility (total marginal benefit) among many product options by only making positive or break even value transactions.For example, let product Z cost 4.50 dollars / unit and have a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.Purchasing 1 unit of product Z is a value transaction of - 4.50 dollars of monetary value and + 5 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of + 0.50 dollars. It is in a consumer's best interest to make this positive value transaction.However, purchasing 2 units of product Z is a value transaction of - 9 dollars of monetary value and + 8 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of - 1 dollars. A consumer will avoid this negative value transaction in a market with many options in favor of other value transactions that are positive or break even in total value payoff.

wrt part 2, missing data, there are several options. Which one you use depends on your objectives, the data and any patterns in the missing data. The simplest choice is to deleted any cases with missing values, see complete.cases in R. This is fine so long as you have sufficient data and there is no pattern in the missing cases, there is of course a downside, you've lost the information in the deleted cases and also you've built a model that cannot handle missing data in the test set. Alternatively you can fill the missing data in (called imputation) with an appropriate value, say mean or median. If you do so, you should create an additional predictor that marks which values were imputed, do this for each predictor seperately. Then you can build your model using the new improved set of predictors (no missing values). If the added predictors are significant, it tells you there may be a pattern in the missing values that can be useful in prediction. There are more complicated methods including multiple imputation (see google). Alternatively (again) some methods can handle missing values natively (for instance random forests). Two references are Little and Rubin - Data Analysis with missing data, though I generally prefer Enders - Applied Missing Data Analysis.Unfortunately which is best depends on your objective and the data. If you do not care about missing values in the test (or real world usage) and you have sufficient data you can delete the cases, else you need to develop an imputation scheme and which is best is data dependent. Which ever you use I recommend adding the extra predictors, it is not uncommon to find patterns in missing bits.

'boot(Xy, myfun, R=1000)' takes the dataframe Xy, the function myfun, and the number R, and estimates the standard error for the value of myfun. The function myfun must be a function of a dataframe and an index vector. Behind the scenes, 'boot' will randomly create R index vectors. For each of the R index vectors (which we never see), 'boot' takes the dataframe, subsets it using that index vector, and computes the value of myfun. At the end of this process there will be R different values for myfun. 'boot' then returns the standard deviation of these R numbers, and this standard deviation will be a good estimate of the standard error for the value of myfun if we could apply myfun to many different samples (which we cannot because we have only the one).

But here are my responses to the questions above:Q: Is the market for housing in San Francisco Pareto efficient? What about deadweight loss? A: The current housing market in San Francisco is not Pareto efficient. One condition that must be met if a market is to be Pareto efficient is this: the marginal benefit, or demand curve, must intersect the marginal cost, or supply curve, at a single point. Enforcing a price ceiling on housing rentals stymies the convergence of supply and demand to a single point of intersection, where MB = MC, by stripping the market's suppliers of the incentive to produce more units until all excess demand is exhausted. A price ceiling set lower than market equilibrium curbs the quantity (and possibly the quality) of rental units supplied to the market as suppliers forego more production despite the presence of excess demand (MB > MC). When a market suffers this ‘lost production' despite excess demand, producer and consumer surpluses are not maximized as they should be to achieve Pareto efficiency. The lost production acts as deadweight on the economy and may render the rent control policy self-defeating from the start.Q: Is there a way to keep the price of housing low while keeping the market efficient? The issue is what we are conditioning on. To calculate the marginal probability of a heads BEFORE the coin flip (not conditioned on the outcome of the coin flip), it is P(H)=0X1/3 + 1/2X1/3 +1X1/3. We need this marginal probability (not conditioned on the outcome) for Bayes' formula: P(HH coin/flipped a heads)=P(flipped a heads/HH coin)*P(HH coin)/P(flipped a heads). In the formula P(flipped a heads) is the marginal probability, which is the probability that we would flip a heads on the first toss (which does not depend on the outcome of that toss). Only the conditional probabilities incorporate information about what actually happened.

We do our best to be flexible with groups and regroup as often as we can, based on performance, but the reality is once in a group, it is difficult to move up. I have heard and read about many practices for mixed ability grouping. It is frustrating be limited in our ability to use them because they take longer than traditional teaching, in my experience, and at least in the short term. Many times what many would consider a traditionally high student will be with a traditionally low student because they both need practice with a particular skill or concept. I do not need to slow down a whole group of students because one needs a lesson, nor do I stop a student from learning something new simply because the others in the group are not ready. In the early 1990s, there was a theory that cold baths might help individuals with chronic fatigue syndrome (also known in the UK as ME or myalgic encephalomyelitis). You had to sit in a cold bath every 1 or 2 days I think, with the duration of sitting in there extending by 1 or 2 minutes each time. I think the theory was to do with resetting or influencing the hypothalamus.It was a bit controversial with people worrying that sitting already ill people in cold water could make things worse for them. But a few people, including the Dr himself I think, said it was beneficial for them. Others did not find it helpful. It does not seem to have caught on or been researched much more since as far as I can tell from a quick search on the internet.However, there was one aspect that always intrigued me. I tried the method myself for a few weeks and I noticed that about 3-4 hours after getting out of the cold bath I would experience a sudden intense rush of warmness all over my body for a couple of minutes. It was a bit like a hot flush I imagine, though it was not uncomfortably hot and did not provoke sweating. It was so noticeable that the first time I looked round to see if other people had also just experienced something changing in the environment, only to realize that it was only me. It was actually quite nice, an extremely cozy sort of warmth - so nice it would have been lovely if it had continued for longer. This occurred despite the fact that I had never felt cold after getting dressed from the bath and had been feeling warm and in a perfectly warm environment for at least 2-3 hours before the warm surge arrived. And the timing was remarkably predictable. I have always been very curious to understand more about the physiology of this effect and would be interested to hear if anyone has heard of this before, and has any explanation. Can anyone explain how we know that the firms' profits will be reduced?Presumably we are in a competitive market initially, so profits are zero and production is at the market equilibrium. Now the government introduces the wage cap. This causes a movement along the labour supply curve - the price of labour has been set, so the quantity supplied will drop accordingly. Firms demand more labour than is available, so there is a deficit of labour, but the cap prevents them from raising wages in response. As the quantity of labour is reduced, the quantity of goods produced is reduced. This reduces the marginal cost of production (diminishing returns on labour mean it's more efficient to produce smaller amounts).At this lower quantity of production, demand is higher than supply, so the price is higher than the marginal cost of producing the goods. This leads to a deadweight loss in the market, but also a profit for the firms. So, lower quantity, higher price, lower marginal costs. Unless we know the elasticities of supply and demand, for both labour and the good(s) being produced, we do not know the relative sizes of these effects. So how can we say whether profits will be higher or lower?

Paraplegics patients suffer from immobility due to spinal cord injury (SCI). They have difficulty in standing-up, due to their lower limb paralysis. To alleviate this, they are trained how to stand–up and compensate the missing action of their lower extremities during the rehabilitation process. The lifting and stabilizing forces are provided by the arm support which requires an abled patient's upper body. For support and balance, a walker frame, parallel bars, simple stationary standing frame or even chair arm rests are normally used. However, people practicing a fully arm support, standing–up, faces later complications of the upper limb joints injuries. In addition to the arm support, standing-up in paraplegia can be facilitated by Functional Electrical Stimulation (FES). It is a promising technology to restore motor functions for paralyzed patients. It adjusts electrical stimuli to induce muscle contraction and the corresponding joint movement. Achieving desired movements require suitable electrical stimulation to the muscles. It has both functional and therapeutic benefits. Restoration standing up would allow paraplegics to reach high objects inaccessible from wheelchair, make transactions at a counter and communicate with other people face to face. Succeed standing up could increase independence, privacy and moral by ruling out the need for an assistant. However, many obstacles are encountered in stimulating the paralyzed neuromuscular system. The control of multiple joints is difficult due to the complexity , nonlinearity , and time-variance of the system (human body) involved. Furthermore, physiological effects such as muscle fatigue, spasticity, and limited force in the stimulated muscle further complicate the control task. FES needs better control strategies to achieve the desired motion. Various studies have been done regarding the sit-to-stand movement during the early 90's. Many control methods have been tested and reported in the FES assisted standing up such as: on/off controller, switching curve controller, Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) controllers, model-based control, fuzzy logic control, and neural network control. In my school we do not track at all (7th-12th) However, everyone does not necessarily take calculus. Students have no choice in their math through grade 10. In grades 11 & 12 they pick classes with guidance from their teachers. The MA state standards and MCAS test says kids have to be able to solve quadratics. I personally agree with the person above that I do not believe that to be a necessary skill. Do all kids need advanced algebra...I do not think so, although my school takes pride in thinking that most of our kids will and should. If we could take away some of the content expectation and focus on the mathematical thinking, we could more easily group heterogeneously. When we track, we put kids on a fixed path that due to prerequisites, they can never veer from. Kids can go down a level, but in math, it is hard to go up a level as usually math is tracked in such a way that kids in upper levels take courses a year early. So if someone gets stronger in math as they age, they have not had the prerequisites to move into the upper level without taking a make up course. With heterogeneous grouping and playing with abilities within a class, all students have the same basic concepts but can develop them to different depths. If a student better understands one concept over another, they can move more deeply into that concept and spend more time on the basics of another. Their pacing varies over the course of the year. The problem right now is that college counselors are pressuring kids to take calculus to be competitive for colleges. I find myself fighting this constantly with the argument, that I'd rather have the student take a course more suited to their current development and do well, then to take a course that looks challenging on paper only to \fail\" or feel like they are failing. There is a top-down affect. High schools want to prepare kids to be successful in college, middle school wants to prepare kids to be successful in high school, etc. But in doing so, we are not necessarily doing what is developmentally appropriate at each grade level. We need to take their brains where they are and work within the developmental confines of them at that point. Learning cannot take place if the work is too easy OR too hard."

The point is to model the mechanism that generated the data, so I'd suggest trying lots of things and seeing what works best. So, beta regression or nonlinear regression are good things to try. But, personally, I'd probably start with something simpler than either of those. It's hard to say without looking at the data and knowing the intended goals of the model, but in general I'd probably suggest tranforming the response and using standard models like linear regression, splines, lasso, whatever, on the transformed response. So, for example, if it really is bounded on an open interval, you can shift and scale the response until it's bounded on (0,1) and the do a logit transform. The transformed response will then be unbounded and the standard models may apply. Of course, if those models do not fit well (e.g., examine the residuals), then you'll need to try something else. For example, you may want to look at folded power transforms for a series of transforms that may work better than logit. If that does not work, then try more complicated approaches.Hope that helps.

Ah, the frequentist vs. bayesian interpretations of confidence intervals!Short answer: neither interpretations suggest a 95% probability of truth for the parameter.Long answer: read on.For the frequentist, there is only one true value for the parameter, which is hidden and we can only approximate based on theories like the Central Limit Theorem. Note that with each random sample set, we expect to get different confidence intervals. Hence, the 95% confidence interval for a parameter indicates that if we repeated the fitting using multiple (& infinite) number of random sample sets, 95% of confidence intervals produced would contain the true parameter. For the bayesian, the parameter (or its estimate) is random and has an associated probability distribution. The 95% **credible** interval communicates the level of belief the experimenter has of the parameter i.e. she is 95% sure of the parameter estimate. Note that it is a subjective belief as the interval is of the posterior distribution based on the experimenter's chosen prior. So, if you are not confused by now, you have not understood it. I will give it a shot...Think about the force you feel when you accelerate - if you accelerate forward in a car you feel a force pulling you back in your seat. Acceleration is any change in velocity relative to the straight line things go in it not affected by other forces. So if you are in that same car, and you turn to the left that's an acceleration too, and you feel a force to the right. The same thing is happening in orbit in space - you would travel in a straight line, but gravity causes your course to bend downward toward the earth. So there is a force you feel away from the earth.In a stable orbit (one that stays the same distance from earth) the outward force you feel from acceleration toward the earth is exactly balanced by the force of gravity pulling you toward the earth. (Neat fact here - one key part Einstein's theories of relativity is this fact - that there is no actual difference between gravity and acceleration). So, since the force from acceleration is exactly the same as the force of gravity, you feel no gravity.Again, by relativity, you are truly experiencing microgravity. it's just that if you stopped in orbit, there would be no force to counteract gravity and you would start getting closer to the earth -- in this case, not a good outcome.In truth, any time you are in free fall, your downward acceleration exactly matches the acceleration from gravity (because that's what free fall is) and you will, as a result, be weightless. In a plane, you can be in free fall for a few seconds. In orbit, because we are moving sideways while we fall, we can (with care) set things up so that we fall at the same rate as the earth's surface falls away from the straight line we'd take without gravity. Since our falling matches the curvature of the earth, we stay in orbit.But fundamentally, it is the fact that we are in free fall that causes the balance of forces that is weightlessness (or more precisely, microgravity)

Imagine for example a data set with one data point per day. If you were to do normal bootstrapping with this, one bootstrap sample might have the data point for 4 May followed by the data point for 25 December followed by the data point for 15 March, and so on. In time series data, subsequent data points are often not entirely independent, so normal bootstrapping would mean losing these dependencies in the noise.To get around that problem at least a little, block bootstrapping groups data points into blocks (of equal size, ideally), and these blocks are then randomly recombined into bootstrap samples. For example, with a data set of one point per day, the block size could be 7, i.e. one week. A bootstrap sample might then have the data points for 27 February to 5 May, followed by the data points for 23 to 30 December, followed by the data points for 11 to 17 March, etc. Some dependencies are still lost (the data of 11 March follows that of 30 December, though it cannot possibly depend on that), but the dependecies within blocks (of 12 March on 11 March, of 13 March on 11 and 12 March, etc.) are retained.

Interesting debate regarding the normality of height. Let me pose the question differently to show that height (and many other measures) cannot be normally distributed, although it can be well approximated as normal. According to the normal distribution, there should be the same proportion of people above the mean as there are below. However, height is >0, whereas it has no maximum (although in reality there could be a limit). So, suppose the mean height is 1.6m, and 0.0001% of the population is 3.3m; if height is normally distributed, then 0.0001% of the population is -0.1m tall, which is not a valid value. The actual % is irrelevant, to the argument.In fact, if you think about the last slide on % response for feelings about math, this MAY be normal ONLY if the mean was 50% and the distribution was unimodal. If the mean is not 50%, then the distribution is not normal, because no one can answer <0% or >100%.But in many cases, people treat the distributions as approximately normal, because it is sufficient to perform the statistics.To summarize, there's probably no population data that's truly normal, but many are approximately normal (or their means are approximately normal), which in itself is sufficient to describe the data and perform statistical tests.

\i.i.d.\" means \"independent and identically distributed\". Normal bootstrapping tacitly assumes that there is no connection between subsequent data points, i.e. that they are independent. This makes sense for a lot of kinds of data: if you sample 100 voters, it does not matter whether John Smith is data point #2 or #99 - his voting behavior is determined by other things (political stance, campagin ads, whatever). A lot of statistical methods require that this is true for the data, so that you can in effect look at a single data point without considering which ones come before/after it.Some kinds of data, however, are NOT independent. If you take the weather of 100 consecutive days, the user ratings of 10 consecutive versions of a product, or other data that develops over time, it matters a great deal what came before a given data point: we all know that today's weather depends a lot on yesterday's weather, and so the weather of day #2 depends a lot on the weather of day #1. Product updates (and thus user satisfaction) depend a lot on user satisfaction with the previous version. By (wrongly) assuming that these data are independent, we lose a lot of the information that determines/predicts a data point.(Block bootstrapping addresses this by sampling not individual data points, but consecutive blocks of data points, so that at least the connections between the points in each block are preserved.)"

We also added a support teacher and modified the lessons slightly, although the students still wrote all the same assessments as the other students. At the end of the year, many of these students were as or more successful than they had been in previous math courses. Even though they were separated into a different class, they felt that they were given extra support so they were willing to work hard to achieve success. The thing is, \education\" is not one single thing. It can be split up into \"elementary education,\" \"secondary education,\" and \"college education.\" And in fact, even \"college education\" can be split into the separate *products*, if you can call it that, of \"public college education,\" \"Ivy League education,\" etc. With that in mind, let's see which of these are public goods.First off, elementary and secondary education are public goods. They are state-funded, and barring the cases of the severely understaffed schools in impoverished areas, they are non-rival and non-excludable (although the students do have the option to drop out after a certain point).As for college education, this is where it gets tricky. A college education is definitely excludable when the product being sold is \"college education at Harvard,\" but not so much when it is \"college education at your local community college.\" It is non-rival if the product is \"college education from online classes,\" but it is rival if the product is \"college education at ________ exclusive university\" (although you could argue that relative to the people already in the university, it is non-rival because attending lectures is free).One unifying factor, though, is that education causes positive externalities. An informed populace has higher wealth, satisfaction, and quality of life. Even those who do not have a higher education benefit from economic increases caused by those who do. The government is therefore subsidizing college education for many incoming college students. Of course, this comes with downsides too: because more students are being subsidized, colleges raise tuition costs, contributing to the rampant problem of student debt. This is, in fact, a negative externality of subsidies given to only certain students. The ones who are not subsidized have to face a higher cost."

This is not a trivial question at all. What you are describing is subsampling, and it's very similar to the bootstrap. The bootstrap is conceptually simpler to implement because a bootstrap sample of size n is roughly as noisy relative to the original sample as the original sample is to the population. Whereas for subsampling you have to decide on which k to use, then you'll often have to make a correction for the fact that your resamples are of different size than your original sample.On the other hand, a subsample of size k is an \honest-to-goodness\" sample of size k from the original population, so there are situations where the bootstrap is known to give you a wrong answer and subsampling (with the appropriate correction) gives you a right answer. For example, bootstrapping would be a wrong way to estimate SD(Max(x_1,...,x_n)) (can you see why?). Whereas subsampling could give you a correct estimate of SD(Max(x_1,...,x_k)) (if k is chosen small enough, obviously k=n is wrong). Then you need to correct that somehow if you want an estimate of SD(Max(x_1,...,x_n))"

In working with students on such problems I abandon the goal of representing the situation in one variable and let them use A, B, and C to start with. I do not see a need to use just one variable, and having 3 variables allows the students to keep the original problem in their head a little longer in working the problem. Jumping right to using 'x' to show the relationship between the three piles is too big a step. So: B = A + 2; C = 4A; A + B + C = 14. Then I talk about the importance of the equals sign. The equals sign is a like a balance scale. The equals sign means you have the same amount of stuff on the left that you do on the right. The equals sign means that the thing on the left (same amount of stuff as the right) can be substituted for the thing on the right anywhere it appears in this problem. And vise versa -- the thing on the right can be substituted for the thing on the left anywhere it appears in the problem. So in this case, you can substitute A + 2 for B anywhere it appears in this situation, and 4A for C anywhere it appears in this situation. So A + B + C = 14 can become A + (A + 2) + (4A) = 14. I will actually write out A + B + C = 14 with lots of space, and then erase the B and write \(A + 2)\" in its place; erase C and write \"(4A)\" in its place. At this point I will point out we now have a mathematical representation of the problem of piles of rocks and how many is in each pile. We check that this mathematical representation truly does represent the problem. Then I ask them for a leap of faith -- to not think about the original problem, but just look at the equation. Now there is one variable in the equation and let's find out what it is -- view it as a puzzle. I let them do any manipulation they want to as long as that manipulation honors the equals sign. We look at the result of each manipulation, asking does it make the equation look less complex -- always keeping in mind that at this point, the goal is to get to \"A = ...\" -- finding out what A is. Once we have A, I have the student look back at the original problem and tell me what we have found out. I ask have we answered the question originally asked? If a single variable, such as x is used, it is easy to think the problem is solved once we find x. My guess is that a lot of market research went into this plan so that Google knows how much storage the average consumer wants or needs and how much they are willing to pay. This is precisely the marginal benefit of online storage for the average consumer. However, Google likely also considered the marginal benefit to special groups of consumers - businessmen, techies, photographers, etc. - people who are likely to want and need more storage than the average consumer. It is important for Google to consider these different groups because the could storage consumer market is not uniform, and I suspect there is opportunity for greater profits within a small but high-demand sector of the market than across the entire market of consumers.For example, 15GB of storage are free to everyone. This free offering will have been driven at least in part by competition - Apple and Amazon both offer free options, and there are a host of smaller cloud storage players out there who also offer free options. However, this is also because the marginal benefit for your average consumer of having cloud storage is probably pretty small at this stage, since it is still a developing market. In terms of willingness to pay, most people simply will not want to pay anything extra for cloud storage. They will just take more time to manage the hard storage available on their devices. This makes even more sense when one considers that the next price point is $1.99 for 100GB of storage. That is A LOT more storage, though still not much if you are someone who works in computing, graphic design, etc. where you are storing large amounts of data on a regular basis. Having said that though, there are a lot of things out there that seem to work for individuals that are hard to support with scientific data - meaning when you combine a group together, the positive, neutral and negative responders cancel each other out. I am not great in the cold, so I personally would not suffer through it for the degree of benefit that has been indicated. But, if you think it is working for you, I would not stop doing it either. Sorry if that sounds wishy washy, but sometimes in physiology the individual response is the most important. You will find that is true for altitude training as well. It seems to work for some, but not others (although in that case we have a slightly better idea of why...). If you are a positive responder then altitude training can give you that 2% benefit you need. If you are not, it could actually make you worse. Keep up the great discussions. If you had a woman who dropped out at 6 months, you cannot ignore the fact that she was at risk of developing the outcome in question during the 6-month period she was in the study. She could have developed the outcome, but did not. That means that her data contribute something to the study. If you keep her data in, the overall likelihood of any patient developing the outcome up until the point she dropped out will be lower than if you took her data out (because her contribution make the denominator higher by 1 person). If the study had planned to end at 6 months, you would have been OK with including her data - so it should be no different if she later drops out because her inclusion affects only the data up to 6 months. You cannot do clinical studies without patients dropping out, so you have to accommodate that fact rather than ignore it.

There are 4 reasons to always have a test data set (assuming you have a large data set with more than 1 MM observations):1. You may be using CV the wrong way (and not know it). As explained in lecture, if you have 1,000 variables and pre-screen them using bi-variate correlations between each x and y, then your CV estimate of test set error may be overly optimistic. 2. The right way to use CV would be to include variable pre-screening at each fold. However, if you have a large data set, doing CV the right way might be computationally intensive. For example, if you do 10-fold CV with 1 MM observations, you are pre-screening the variables 10 times where **each** iteration would use 900,000 observations to pre-screen 1,000 variables. If you had a 70% training/30% test splilt, you would prescreen the variables once on 700,000 training observations.3. If you use CV to estimate tuning parameters **and** use CV to estimate test set error, your CV test set error may be overly optimistic. I often use CV to choose tuning parameters, but use a test set to estimate test set error.4. Comparing CV test set errors between two models (e.g., lasso vs. trees) may be problematic unless you correctly set the seed values. By default, 10-fold CV randomly assigns an observation to one fold. If you run 10-fold CV repeatedly, an observation might end up in different folds. For example, you run cv.glmnet(), observation 1 might be in fold 9. If you run cv.tree() observation 1 might be in fold 10. The CV test set errors are not comparable because the compositions of the folds are different! You can avoid this (I think) by setting the same seed value right before running each cv function.

In the article, “New Lessons: The Power of Educating Adolescent Girls,” Lloyd makes an important argument regarding the importance of non-formal education. In developing countries, where young and adolescent girls do not fully attend formal or state-run schools, non-formal schools or education facilities have emerged. These non-formal schools are run by NGOs, donors or local communities to provide children and adolescents access to an education that they may not otherwise have. I was lucky enough to volunteer at an NGO-run non-formal school in Udaipur, India. The school was directed towards gypsy children whose families often moved or who could not afford to have children leave for a majority of the day to attend state-run schools. Although state-run primary education in India is free, poor families often require their children, especially girls, to stay home and work instead of getting an education. Non-formal schools offer the opportunity for these children to attend school because they are often run at hours that can accommodate the children's work day. The school I volunteered at ran from 2pm-5pm. Attendance was taken everyday and children were encouraged to attend daily through incentives such as a daily healthy meal and through threat of not being allowed back if they missed more than a week of school. I noticed that there were more girls than boys between the ages of 5-8, however it was extremely evident that more boys aged 9-13 attended than girls. Non-formal education facilities, such as this school in Udaipur, are important for children who cannot access state-run schools. However, these facilities also require the attention of the global community in order to encourage and facilitate the attendance of adolescent girls. Through offering schooling at different times throughout the day and accommodating to the needs of these girls, improved access to education could be achieved. I agree with Lloyd in her suggestion that surveys be conducted on attendance in non-formal schools as well as in her suggestion that the non-formal sector and formal sector should be well integrated. Through the help of donors and volunteers, the non-formal sector could enable young and adolescent girls to attend formal secondary and post-secondary institutions.

When you type \"x\", for example, R knows exactly which vector you are talking about.This is rare case!In most examples (and in real life, usually) the parameters used in your formula are actually columns (vectors) in a **data frame**. Just specifying the column name alone is not enough for R to know what you are talking about--you have to *also* tell it the data frame to look in.So let's say `x` and `y` *were* in a data frame called, for example, `foo`. I would say that Opportunity Cost is in the eye of the beholder, and your view of the rule depends on who you are.For those young 18 year-olds who want to play in the NBA above everything else, the opportunity cost is to lose a year of professional pay/experience. These folks will feel a high Opportunity Cost being imposed on them - they will not like the rule.For those young 18 year-olds who want an education in addition to the NBA career, the opportunity cost of losing the professional pay/experience will likely be outweighed by the value of education. For them, college ball experience may be a very suitable substitute, and they may actually stick it out and graduate. These folks will not feel the imposition of a substantive Opportunity Cost, especially if they are OK with a delayed start in their pro careers.Edited: From the perspective of the colleges/universities, there's an opportunity cost of losing the best players to the NBA, in lieu of having that talent grow in college ball. Colleges would probably prefer to keep that notable talent because it helps their recruiting, both for sports and otherwise. Certainly this is true for football. For the NBA industry, who would not have access for one year (or more) to young 18-year old players with enormous talent, the Opportunity Cost is the lack of access to someone who may have been instrumental in developing a winning team in that particular year (read: big $$$). However, this cost is counter-balanced by the annual sustainment of an improved college-experienced pool of NBA candidates who might be better able to handle the pressures of pro ball. It's a trade space - short term advantage for quick bucks vs. longer term advantage for better return on investment. Since the rule nudges the NBA industry away from the quick bucks (at the cost of exploiting the youngest people), I am all for it, so I vote to increase the time. From an economic standpoint, my suspicion is that the the moneymaking viability of the NBA will survive just fine, even if the players are a bit older before they are allowed to play. (EDIT: On a purely practical note, whenever you bother to find the standard error of a statistic, you probably should be assuming the sampling distribution of the statistic is approximately normal because otherwise the standard error is not a terribly useful summary of the shape of the distribution and hence not a good measure of the uncertainty in the statistic.)Remember that in linear regression we are assuming that $hat{Y}=hat{f}(X)$ is a linear (in the parameters) function of $X$ (i.e., it is an estimate of $E[Y|X]$ under an assumption about the functional form: $E[Y|X]=f(X)$). Once we have a set of data $(X_i,Y_i)$, we can estimate the parameters and hence the functional form $hat{f}(X)=hat{Y}$ as a function of $X$. Then, we can estimate the mean value of the response $Y$ on a new explanatory value $X_{new}$ as $hat{Y}_{new}=hat{f}(X_{new})$, based on the observed data $(X_i,Y_i)$. Also based on the same observed data, we can estimate the standard error of $hat{Y}_{new}$ using the formula you gave in your first post above (which is based on the assumption of normality). Alternately, we can estimate the standard error of $hat{Y}(X_{new})$ by taking lots (say $B$) of bootstrap samples of the observed data $(X_i,Y_i)$, fitting the model to each bootstrap sample, calculating $hat{Y}_{new,j}=hat{f}_j(X_{new})$ for $j=1cdots B$, and then finding the standard deviation of $hat{Y}_{new,j}$ for $j=1cdots B$. Note however that if the sampling distribution of $hat{Y}_{new}$ is not close to being normal (e.g., if the histogram of $hat{Y}_{new,j}$ is not well approximated by a normal distribution) , the standard error of $hat{Y}_{new}$ will not be useful as a summary of uncertainty (e.g., the CIs calculated from it will not have the nominal coverage). In that case, it would be better to form a CI on $hat{Y}_{new}$ using quantiles of the sampling distribution. To answer question 1,Let \A\" be the original set of data and \"B\" to be a bootstrapped sample from A. Naturally B is a subset of A and from 36/51 in the lecture notes on trees, B has on average 2/3 of the values in A. Thus, we can use the other 1/3 to do validating.Now one might be quick to jump in and say that this is 3-fold cross-validation but this is not exactly. In k-fold cross validation, we slice the original sample up into k different parts and then do the validating by building the model on all except one part. In OOB however, notice that although B is approximately 2/3 of A, the composition is not deterministic. Also, in k-fold cross validation, we need only to perform k computation and average them. On the other hand, OOB does it as many times as the number of Bootstrap samples required.All in all, OOB is some kind of cross validation though we cannot directly pin point the number of folds it is doing. Since it is naturally to add an additional prediction step for the other 1/3 of the sample that is not included in the bootstrapped sample, it is only computationally wise to just compute it internally. Rest assure, it is definitely an unbiased estimate of the errors as expectation is linear and thus averaging it over B estimates do not matter versus K estimates. The only thing that will differ could be the estimated variance of the error rate since variance generally decreases as the number of samples increase (e.g. for variance of mean is (sigma^2)/n). The equipment at each end is effected by extreme temperatures and/or extreme humidity causing voltage drifts. Therefore sometimes the letter received by B differs from the true one transmitted by A. Similar to morse code only in my example errors are normally distributed around the true letter. In other words, if the true letter is \O\", the most likely errors states are \"N\" and \"P\". If B constructs 95% confidence intervals showing that the letter is between \"M\" and \"Q\", he CAN say that based on past experience he is 95% percent certain that he put his intervals on either side of the the true letter. He CAN NOT say that the unknown letter has a 95% chance of being between \"M\" and \"Q\". If the true letter, unknown to B, is \"O\", \"O\" is either between \"M\" and \"Q\" or it is not. \"O\" does not change its position in the alphabet randomly."

One thing that has worked in my elementary school is the introduction of daily word problems. Our administration believes that using math story problems in our classrooms can give every student a chance to develop understanding of basic math concepts. This has been highly successful. First, we introduce a real life situation based on our math objective. We then have the students tell each other the story and what the specific task is. We then have the students use unifix cubes, drawings, numerical representations of how they solve the problem, using at least one representation that can be put down on paper. This lets all level of achievers to use whatever forum they want. When higher students finish, we give them the task to solve it another way and show their thinking. As students work individually, the teacher goes around and asks students what they are showing (how they are making sense of their thinking) and selects three students to present their strategies to the class. These presentations are to be from simple to more complex so that all students can see/relate their thinking to another way of solving the problem. This has been highly successful in our school practices and has shown us that all students can do math. I found that at the end of doing this for an entire year, most if not all students were able to express their math thinking with ease and were more than eager to share and be presenters to the class. I noticed doing daily math word problems also obliterated the anxiety that often accompanies such problems. Last year, one of my students exclaimed, \I am not afraid of story problems anymore.\" This was all the proof I needed. I am continuing this practice!"
